items.name: Skeip biech
items.text: Bee skep: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A beehive is an enclosed structure in which honey bees raise their young and produce honey as part of their seasonal cycle.

items.name: Toitchaiteoir biech
items.text: Bee smoker: earliest widespread use 1873 (USA). A bee smoker (usually called simply a smoker or a smokepot) is a device used in beekeeping to calm honey bees.

items.name: Meisín miela a bhainti
items.text: Honey extractor: earliest widespread use 1865 (Austria). A honey extractor is a mechanical device used in extraction of honey from honeycombs.

items.name: Pouta kókairechta
items.text: Cooking pot: earliest widespread use c. 18000 BC (East Asia). A cooking pot (saucepan in British English) is a large bowl that is heated in order to cook the food inside it.

items.name: Katur
items.text: Cauldron: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). A cauldron (or a caldron) is a large pot or kettle used for cooking or boiling, typically over an open fire.

items.name: Ófau oldundach
items.text: Dutch oven: earliest widespread use 1700s (Netherlands). A Dutch oven, Dutch pot (US English), or casserole dish (international) is a thick-walled cooking pot with a tight-fitting lid.

items.name: Panda friuchta
items.text: Frying pan: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Mesopotamia). A frying pan, also called frypan or skillet, is a flat-bottomed cookware used for frying, searing and browning foods.

items.name: Wouk
items.text: Wok: earliest widespread use Han dynasty (China). A wok (simplified Chinese: 镬; traditional Chinese: 鑊; pinyin: huò; Cantonese Yale: wohk) is a deep round-bottomed cooking pan of either indigenous Chinese origin or derived from the South Asian karahi.

items.name: Sáspánu
items.text: Saucepan: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A saucepan is one of the basic forms of cookware (not technically a pan), in the form of a round cooking vessel, typically 3.5 to 4 inches (90 to 100 mm) deep, and wide enough to hold at least 1 US quart (33 imp fl oz; 950 ml) of water, with sizes typically ranging up to 4 US quarts (130 imp fl oz;

items.name: Pouta marakundach
items.text: Tagine: earliest widespread use c. 800 (Morocco). A tagine or tajine, also tajin or tagin (Arabic: طاجين, romanized: ṭajīn) is a Maghrebi cuisine stew, named for the earthenware pot in which it is cooked.

items.name: Pouta kré
items.text: Clay cooking pot: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Clay pot cooking is a process of cooking food in a ceramic pot.

items.name: Kiseán gaili
items.text: Bamboo steamer: earliest widespread use Neolithic (China). Bamboo steamers, called zhēnglóng (蒸籠) in Chinese, are a type of food steamer made of bamboo.

items.name: Kókairi brúu
items.text: Pressure cooker: earliest widespread use 1679 (France). A pressure cooker is a sealed vessel used for cooking food with the use of high pressure steam and water or a water-based liquid, in a process called pressure cooking.

items.name: Kitel
items.text: Kettle: earliest widespread use 1700s (Britain). A kettle, sometimes called a tea kettle or teakettle, is a device specialized for boiling water, commonly with a lid, spout, and handle.

items.name: Tiepota
items.text: Teapot: earliest widespread use c. 1500 (China). A teapot is a vessel used for steeping tea leaves or a herbal mix in boiling or near-boiling water and serving the resulting infusion called tea; usually put in a teacup.

items.name: Samavur
items.text: Samovar: earliest widespread use 1700s (Russia). A samovar (Russian: самовар, IPA: [səmɐˈvar] , lit. 'self-brewer') is a metal container traditionally used to heat and boil water.

items.name: Poiti chaifi
items.text: Coffee pot: earliest widespread use 1500s (Ottoman). A coffeemaker, coffee maker or coffee machine is a cooking appliance used to brew coffee.

items.name: Poiti kaifé toirkech
items.text: Cezve: earliest widespread use 1500s (Ottoman). A cezve (Turkish: cezve, pronounced [dʒezˈve] ; Serbo-Croatian: džezva / џезва; Arabic: جِذوَة), also ibriki/briki (Greek: μπρίκι), srjep (Armenian: սրճեփ), rakwa (Arabic: ركوة), ghallaya (Arabic: غلاية), or kanaka (Arabic: كَنَكَة), is a small long-handled pot with a pouring lip designed specifical

items.name: Poiti mouka
items.text: Moka pot: earliest widespread use 1933 (Italy). The moka pot is a stove-top or electric coffee maker that brews coffee by passing hot water driven by vapor pressure and heat-driven gas expansion through ground coffee.

items.name: Peirkuladóir
items.text: Percolator: earliest widespread use 1810 (France). A coffee percolator is a type of pot used for the brewing of coffee by continually cycling the boiling or nearly boiling brew through the grounds using gravity until the required strength is reached.

items.name: Poiti dhúbailti
items.text: Double boiler: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bain-marie (English:  BAN-mə-REE, French: [bɛ̃ maʁi]), also known as a water bath or double boiler, a type of heated bath, is a piece of equipment used in science, industry, and cooking to heat materials gently or to keep materials warm over a period of time.

items.name: Plátau bákála
items.text: Baking sheet: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A sheet pan, also referred to as baking tray, baking sheet, or baking pan, is a flat, rectangular metal pan placed in an oven and used for baking pastries such as bread rolls, cookies, sheet cakes, Swiss rolls, and pizzas.

items.name: Panda róstau
items.text: Roasting pan: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A roasting pan or dripping pan is a piece of cookware used for roasting meat in an oven, either with or without vegetables or other ingredients.

items.name: Greidel
items.text: Griddle: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A griddle, also called a girdle in Scotland, is a cooking device consisting mainly of a broad, usually flat cooking surface.

items.name: Plaitíni tortilda
items.text: Comal: earliest widespread use Pre-Columbian (Mesoamerica). A comal is a smooth, flat griddle typically used in Mexico, Central America, and parts of South America, to cook tortillas and arepas, toast spices and nuts, sear meat, and generally prepare food.

items.name: Taundúr
items.text: Tandoor: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Indus). A tandoor ( or , Hindi: [t̪ən̪d̪uːɾ]) is a large vase-shaped oven, usually made of clay.

items.name: Oigend auráin
items.text: Beehive oven: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A masonry oven, colloquially known as a brick oven or stone oven, is an oven consisting of a baking chamber made of fireproof brick, concrete, stone, clay (clay oven), or cob (cob oven).

items.name: Spíki róstau
items.text: Roasting spit: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Rotisserie, also known as spit-roasting, is a style of roasting where meat is skewered on a spit – a long, solid rod used to hold food while it is being cooked over a fire in a fireplace or over a campfire, or roasted in an oven.

items.name: Trípéaud
items.text: Trivet: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A trivet () is an object placed between a serving dish, bowl, pot, or pan and a dining table, usually to protect the table from heat damage.

items.name: Krú krochta
items.text: Pot hook: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A trammel hook is an adjustable hook used to suspend objects at variable heights.

items.name: Iarund vaifilíi
items.text: Waffle iron: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A waffle iron or waffle maker is a kitchen utensil used to cook waffles between two hinged metal plates.

items.name: Poupadóir aurán róstau
items.text: Popcorn popper: earliest widespread use 1800s (USA). A popcorn maker (also called a popcorn copper) is a machine used to make popcorn.

items.name: Tóstaeri
items.text: Toaster: earliest widespread use 1893 (Scotland). A toaster is a small electric appliance that uses radiant heat to cook sliced bread into toast.

items.name: Pauna mufun
items.text: Muffin tin: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A muffin or cupcake tray  is a mold in which muffins or cupcakes are baked.

items.name: Panda buindt
items.text: Bundt pan: earliest widespread use 1950 (USA). A Bundt cake is a cake that is baked in a Bundt pan, shaping it into a distinctive donut shape.

items.name: Panda skoiti
items.text: Springform pan: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A springform pan is a type of bakeware that features sides that can be removed from the base.

items.name: Panda káka
items.text: Cake pan: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). Cookware and bakeware is food preparation equipment, such as cooking pots (saucepan in British English), frying pans, baking sheets etc.

items.name: Miasu pieóg
items.text: Pie dish: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A pie is a baked dish which is usually made of a pastry dough casing that contains a filling of various sweet or savoury ingredients.

items.name: Soitech kasuról
items.text: Casserole dish: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A casserole (French: diminutive of casse, from Provençal cassa, meaning 'saucepan') is a kind of large, deep pan or bowl used for cooking a variety of dishes in the oven; it is also a category of foods cooked in such a vessel.

items.name: Teiríni
items.text: Terrine: earliest widespread use Medieval (France). Terrine may refer to:

items.name: Ramakuin
items.text: Ramekin: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). A ramekin (, ; also spelled ramequin) is a small dish used for culinary purposes.

items.name: Panda paelda
items.text: Paella pan: earliest widespread use 1800s (Spain). Paella ( py-EL-ə,  pah-AY-yə; Valencian: [paˈeʎa]; Spanish: [paˈeʎa] or [paˈeʝa]) is a rice dish originally from the Valencian Community.

items.name: Poiti foundue
items.text: Fondue pot: earliest widespread use 1900s (Switzerland). Fondue (UK:  FON-dew, US:  fon-DEW, French: [fɔ̃dy], Swiss Standard German: [fɔ̃ːˈdyː] ; Italian: fonduta) is a Swiss dish of melted cheese and wine served in a communal pot (caquelon or fondue pot) over a portable stove (réchaud) heated with a candle or spirit lamp, and eaten by dipping bread and s

items.name: Griel rakletti
items.text: Raclette grill: earliest widespread use 1900s (Switzerland). Raclette (, French: [ʁaklɛt] ) is a dish of Swiss origin, also popular in other countries, based on heating cheese and scraping off the melted part, then typically served with boiled potatoes.

items.name: Grild barbaikéi
items.text: Barbecue grill: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A barbecue grill or barbeque grill (known as a barbecue in Canada and barbecue or barbie in Australia and New Zealand) is a device that cooks food by applying heat from below.

items.name: Hiebachi
items.text: Hibachi: earliest widespread use Heian (Japan). The hibachi (火鉢, 'fire bowl') is a traditional Japanese heating device.

items.name: Kamado
items.text: Kamado: earliest widespread use Kofun (Japan). A kamado (竈, 竃 or 灶) is a traditional Japanese wood- or charcoal-fueled cook stove.

items.name: Taubún
items.text: Tabun oven: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Levant). A tabun oven, or simply tabun (also transliterated taboon, from the Arabic: طابون), is a portable clay oven, shaped like a truncated cone.

items.name: Oigend taulún
items.text: Earth oven: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). An earth oven, ground oven or cooking pit is one of the simplest and most ancient cooking structures.

items.name: Báikeir kré
items.text: Clay baker: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). Roman cuisine is the cooking traditions and practices of the Italian city of Rome.

items.name: Kókairi rísu
items.text: Rice cooker: earliest widespread use 1955 (Japan). A rice cooker or rice steamer is an automated kitchen appliance designed to boil or steam rice.

items.name: Kókairi mald
items.text: Slow cooker: earliest widespread use 1936 (USA). A slow cooker (also known as a crock-pot after a trademark owned by Sunbeam Products, but sometimes used generically in the English-speaking world) is a countertop electrical cooking appliance used to simmer at a lower temperature than other cooking methods, such as baking, boiling, and frying.

items.name: Gaetuiri miutuil
items.text: Metal steamer: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Steaming is a method of cooking using steam.

items.name: Boska dieteig
items.text: Meat smoker: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A smokehouse (North American) or smokery (British) is a building where meat or fish is cured with smoke.

items.name: Maidm
items.text: Butter churn: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Churn may refer to:

items.name: Brúchánu káisi
items.text: Cheese press: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A cheese press is a device for pressing whey from curds when making cheese.

items.name: Múnlau káisi
items.text: Cheese mould: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). Cheesemaking (or caseiculture) is the art of making cheese.

items.name: Stólánu blieguin
items.text: Milking stool: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A stool is a raised seat commonly supported by three or four legs, but with neither armrests nor a backrest.

items.name: Tuod tochuilti
items.text: Mattock: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A mattock () is a hand tool used for digging, prying, and chopping.

items.name: Sluosaid
items.text: Shovel: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A shovel is a tool used for digging, lifting, and moving bulk materials, such as soil, coal, gravel, snow, sand, or ore.

items.name: Spádu
items.text: Spade: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A spade is a tool primarily for digging, consisting of a long handle and blade, typically with the blade narrower and flatter than the common shovel.

items.name: Land lám
items.text: Garden trowel: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A trowel is a small hand tool used for digging, applying, smoothing, or moving small amounts of viscous or particulate material.

items.name: Adurk
items.text: Hoe: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A hoe is an ancient and versatile agricultural and horticultural hand tool used to shape soil, remove weeds, clear soil, and harvest root crops.

items.name: Kliad
items.text: Rake: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A rake (Old English raca, cognate with Dutch hark, German Rechen or Harke, from the root meaning 'to scrape together', 'heap up') is a broom for outside use; a versatile horticultural implement consisting of a toothed bar fixed transversely to a handle, or tines fixed to a handle, and used to collec

items.name: Kráfóg
items.text: Pitchfork: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A pitchfork or hay fork is an agricultural tool used to pitch loose material, such as hay, straw, manure, or leaves.

items.name: Fork féier
items.text: Hay fork: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Hayfork may refer to:

items.name: Spiel
items.text: Scythe: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). A scythe (, ) is an agricultural hand-tool for mowing grass or harvesting crops.

items.name: Korrán
items.text: Sickle: earliest widespread use c. 10000 BC (Levant). A sickle, bagging hook, reaping-hook or grasshook is a single-handed agricultural tool designed with variously curved blades and typically used for harvesting or reaping grain crops, or cutting succulent forage chiefly for feeding livestock.

items.name: Korrán láimi
items.text: Billhook: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). A billhook or bill hook is a versatile cutting tool used widely in agriculture and forestry for cutting woody material such as shrubs, small trees and branches.

items.name: Klaím mhóru
items.text: Machete: earliest widespread use 1500s (Americas). A machete (; Spanish pronunciation: [maˈtʃete]) is a broad blade originating from Central America.

items.name: Siusúr gairdíni
items.text: Secateurs: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). Pruning shears, also called hand pruners (in American English) or secateurs (in British English), are a type of scissors used for plants.

items.name: Siusúr kaerach
items.text: Sheep shears: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). Shears may refer to:

items.name: Siusúr klaí
items.text: Hedge shears: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A hedge trimmer, shrub trimmer, or bush trimmer is a gardening tool or machine used for trimming (cutting, pruning) hedges or solitary shrubs (bushes).

items.name: Baurra rota
items.text: Wheelbarrow: earliest widespread use c. 100 AD (China). A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled load-bearing vehicle, usually with just one wheel, designed to be pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear.

items.name: Krand aruiri
items.text: Ard plough: earliest widespread use c. 4000 BC (Mesopotamia). The ard, ard plough, or scratch plough is a simple light plough without a mouldboard.

items.name: Aruiri klatach
items.text: Moldboard plough: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A plough or plow (US) (both pronounced ) is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing seed or planting.

items.name: Fiersaid
items.text: Harrow: earliest widespread use Roman (Eurasia). In agriculture, a harrow is a farm implement used for surface tillage.

items.name: Tiumuntán sílu
items.text: Seed drill: earliest widespread use 1701 (England). A seed drill is a device used in agriculture that sows seeds for crops by positioning them in the soil and burying them to a specific depth while being dragged by a tractor.

items.name: Suoiteán
items.text: Threshing flail: earliest widespread use Medieval (Eurasia). Flail may refer to:

items.name: Kriatur
items.text: Winnowing basket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Winnowing is a process by which chaff is separated from grain.

items.name: Krand púiri
items.text: Ox yoke: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A yoke is a wooden beam used between a pair of oxen or other animals to enable them to pull together on a load when working in pairs, as oxen usually do.

items.name: Boikéad baindi
items.text: Milk pail: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Pail may refer to:

items.name: Skriú airkiméides
items.text: Archimedes' screw: earliest widespread use c. 250 BC (Greece). An Archimedes' screw is a hydraulic machine composed of an outer cylinder and an inner cylinder with helical blades.

items.name: Krand oiski mieáchun
items.text: Shaduf: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Mesopotamia). A shadoof (or shaduf, well pole, well sweep, sweep, swape, or simply a lift) is a tool that is used to lift water from a well or another water source onto land or into another waterway or basin.

items.name: Rod oiski
items.text: Noria: earliest widespread use Ancient (Levant). A noria (Arabic: ناعورة, romanized: nā‘ūra) is a hydropowered scoop wheel used to lift water into a small aqueduct, either for the purpose of irrigation or to supply water to cities and villages.

items.name: Kanda oiski
items.text: Watering can: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A watering can (or watering pot or watering jug) is a portable container, usually with a handle and a funnel, used to water plants by hand.

items.name: Krúb kapuild
items.text: Horseshoe: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A horseshoe is a piece of equestrian equipment that protects a horse hoof from wear.

items.name: Rauspa krúibeora
items.text: Farrier's rasp: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A farrier is a specialist in farriery: equine hoof care, including the trimming and balancing of horses' hooves and the placing of shoes on their hooves when necessary.

items.name: Piukán krúibi
items.text: Hoof pick: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Horse grooming is hygienic care given to a horse, or a process by which the horse's physical appearance is enhanced for horse shows or other types of competition.

items.name: Dialdait
items.text: Saddle: earliest widespread use c. 700 BC (Eurasia). A saddle is a supportive structure for a rider of an animal, fastened to an animal's back by a girth.

items.name: Stiurap
items.text: Stirrup: earliest widespread use c. 300 (China). A stirrup is one of a pair of light frames or rings attached to the saddle of a riding animal (usually a horse or other equine, such as a mule) by a strap (often called a stirrup leather) that holds its rider's foot, aiding in their mounting and support.

items.name: Srianu
items.text: Bridle: earliest widespread use c. 3500 BC (Eurasia). A bridle is a piece of equipment used to direct a horse.

items.name: Halstur
items.text: Halter: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A halter or headcollar is headgear placed on animals used to lead or tie up livestock and, occasionally, other animals; it fits behind the ears (behind the poll), and around the muzzle.

items.name: Klog bóu
items.text: Cowbell: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A cowbell (or cow bell) is a bell worn around the neck of free-roaming livestock so herders can keep track of an animal via the sound of the bell when the animal is grazing out of view in hilly landscapes or vast plains.

items.name: Bauta tochuilti
items.text: Digging stick: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A digging stick, sometimes called a yam stick, is a wooden implement used primarily by subsistence-based cultures to dig out underground food such as roots and tubers, tilling the soil, or burrowing animals and anthills.

items.name: Biur plaundála
items.text: Dibber: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A dibber or dibble or dibbler is a pointed wooden stick for making holes in the ground so that seeds, seedlings or small bulbs can be planted.

items.name: Korrán kliatánach
items.text: Grain cradle: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A grain cradle or cradle, is a modification to a standard scythe to keep the cut grain stems aligned.

items.name: Míntilder
items.text: Cultivator: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A cultivator is a piece of agricultural equipment used for secondary tillage.

items.name: Kliad dhiuska
items.text: Disc harrow: earliest widespread use 1800s (United States). A disk harrow is a harrow whose cutting edges are a row of concave metal discs, which may be scalloped or set at an oblique angle.

items.name: Rólóier
items.text: Cultipacker: earliest widespread use 1900s (United States). A cultipacker is a piece of agricultural equipment that crushes dirt clods, removes air pockets, and presses down small stones, forming a smooth, firm seedbed.

items.name: Plauntóir arbuir
items.text: Corn planter: earliest widespread use 1850s (United States). A planter is a farm implement, usually towed behind a tractor, that sows (plants) seeds in rows throughout a field.

items.name: Buonuiri meikniúil
items.text: Mechanical reaper: earliest widespread use 1831 (United States). A reaper is a farm implement that reaps (cuts and often also gathers) crops at harvest when they are ripe.

items.name: Buonuiri kiengultóir
items.text: Reaper-binder: earliest widespread use 1870s (United States). The reaper-binder, or binder, is a farm implement that improved upon the simple reaper.

items.name: Meisín bainti féier
items.text: Mowing machine: earliest widespread use 1830s (United States). A mower is a person or machine that cuts (mows) grass or other plants that grow on the ground.

items.name: Ráka féier
items.text: Horse-drawn hay rake: earliest widespread use 1800s (United States). A hay rake is an agricultural rake used to collect cut hay or straw into windrows for later collection (e.g.

items.name: Skaipeoir féier
items.text: Tedder: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). Tedder is a surname.

items.name: Skaipeoir aeilech
items.text: Manure spreader: earliest widespread use 1860s (United States). A manure spreader, muck spreader, or honey wagon is an agricultural machine used to distribute manure over a field as a fertilizer.

items.name: Bailiteoir féier
items.text: Hay baler: earliest widespread use 1872 (United States). A baler, or hay baler, is a piece of farm machinery used to compress a cut and raked crop (such as hay, cotton, flax straw, salt marsh hay, or silage) into compact bales that are easy to handle, transport, and store.

items.name: Meisín buoilti
items.text: Threshing machine: earliest widespread use 1786 (Scotland). A threshing machine or a thresher is a piece of farm equipment that separates grain seed from the stalks and husks.

items.name: Gien kadáis
items.text: Cotton gin: earliest widespread use 1793 (United States). A cotton gin—meaning "cotton engine"—is a machine that quickly and easily separates cotton fibers from their seeds, enabling much greater productivity than manual cotton separation.

items.name: Gierrtóir káitníni
items.text: Chaff cutter: earliest widespread use 1700s (England). A chaff cutter is a mechanical device for cutting straw or hay into small pieces before being mixed together with other forage and fed to horses and cattle.

items.name: Meisín krú
items.text: Milking machine: earliest widespread use 1860 (United States). Automatic milking is the milking of dairy animals, especially of dairy cattle, without human labour.

items.name: Einsini tarruingti gaili
items.text: Steam traction engine: earliest widespread use 1850s (England). A traction engine is a steam-powered tractor used to move heavy loads on roads, plough ground or to provide power at a chosen location.

items.name: Tarrakóir
items.text: Tractor: earliest widespread use 1892 (United States). A tractor is an engineering vehicle specifically designed to deliver a high tractive effort (or torque) at slow speeds, for the purposes of hauling a trailer or machinery, such as that used in agriculture, mining or construction.

items.name: Tarrakóir lourgaí
items.text: Crawler tractor: earliest widespread use 1904 (United States). Continuous track or tracked treads are a system of vehicle propulsion used in tracked vehicles, running on a continuous band of treads or track plates driven by two or more wheels.

items.name: Tarrakóir sieúlach
items.text: Two-wheel tractor: earliest widespread use 1910s (Europe). Two-wheel tractor or walking tractor (French: motoculteur, Russian: мотоблок (motoblok), German: Einachsschlepper) are generic terms understood in the US and in parts of Europe to represent a single-axle tractor, which is a tractor with one axle, self-powered and self-propelled, which can pull and power various farm implements such as a trailer, cultivator or harrow, a plough, or various seeders and harvesters.

items.name: Plaundóir rísi
items.text: Rice transplanter: earliest widespread use 1960s (Japan). A rice transplanter is a specialized transplanter fitted to transplant rice seedlings onto paddy fields.

items.name: Buointeoir komchenguilti
items.text: Combine harvester: earliest widespread use 1835 (United States). The modern combine harvester, also called a combine, is a machine designed to harvest a variety of cultivated seeds.

items.name: Buointeoir bieta
items.text: Forage harvester: earliest widespread use 1930s (United States). A forage harvester – also known as a silage harvester, forager or chopper – is a farm implement that harvests forage plants to make silage.

items.name: Piukadóir kadáis
items.text: Cotton picker: earliest widespread use 1944 (United States). A cotton picker is either a machine that harvests cotton, or a person who picks ripe cotton fibre from the plants.

items.name: Piukadóir arbuir
items.text: Corn picker: earliest widespread use 1900s (United States). A corn picker is an agricultural machine used to harvest corn leaving the whole ear intact rather than shelling the kernels off like a conventional combine.

items.name: Buointeoir siúkra
items.text: Sugarcane harvester: earliest widespread use 1940s (Australia). A sugarcane harvester is a large piece of agricultural machinery used to harvest and partially process sugarcane.

items.name: Buointeoir prátauí
items.text: Potato harvester: earliest widespread use 1900s (United States). Potato harvesters are machines that harvest potatoes.

items.name: Spréauyer baurr
items.text: Crop sprayer: earliest widespread use 1920s (United States). A sprayer is a device used to spray a liquid, where sprayers are commonly used for projection of water, weed killers, crop performance materials, pest maintenance chemicals, as well as manufacturing and production line ingredients.

items.name: Oiskiseoir láraiti
items.text: Center-pivot irrigator: earliest widespread use 1948 (United States). Center-pivot irrigation (sometimes called central-pivot irrigation), also called water-wheel and circle irrigation, is a method of crop irrigation in which equipment rotates around a pivot and crops are watered with sprinklers.

items.name: Dróien talmaíochta
items.text: Agricultural drone: earliest widespread use 2010s (Japan). An agricultural drone is an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) used in agriculture operations, mostly in yield optimization by monitoring crop growth, aerial seeding and crop protection.

items.name: Roubót talmaíochta
items.text: Agricultural robot: earliest widespread use 2010s (Worldwide). An agricultural robot is a robot deployed for agricultural purposes.

items.name: Skaradán uochtuir
items.text: Cream separator: earliest widespread use 1878 (Sweden). Cream separation, milk separation, milk skimming, or milk creaming is the separation of whole milk into cream and skimmed milk.

items.name: Swatóir
items.text: Swather: earliest widespread use 1950s (Canada). A swather (North America), or windrower (Australia and rest of world), is a farm implement that cuts hay or small grain crops and forms them into a windrow for drying.

items.name: Biur tini
items.text: Fire drill: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A fire drill is a method of practicing how a building should evacuate in the event of a fire or other emergencies.

items.name: Triebán tini
items.text: Fire plough: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Oceania). A fire plough (or fire plow) is a firelighting tool.

items.name: Flient augus kruoch
items.text: Flint and steel: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A fire striker or fire steel is a tool used in fire making, consisting of a piece of steel that can be struck against a flint, chert, or other hard rock in order to generate sparks.

items.name: Boska smoleig
items.text: Tinderbox: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A tinderbox, or patch box, is a container made of wood or metal containing flint, firesteel, and tinder (typically charcloth, but possibly a small quantity of dry, finely divided fibrous matter such as hemp), used together to help kindle a fire.

items.name: Méirdes
items.text: Friction match: earliest widespread use 1826 (England). A match is a tool for starting a fire.

items.name: Laustóir
items.text: Pocket lighter: earliest widespread use 1823 (Germany). A lighter is a portable device which uses mechanical or electrical means to create a controlled flame, and can be used to ignite a variety of flammable items, such as cigarettes,  butane gas, fireworks, candles, or campfires.

items.name: Fuingas smoleig
items.text: Tinder bracket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Europe). Fomes fomentarius (commonly known as the tinder fungus, false tinder fungus, hoof fungus, tinder conk, tinder polypore or ice man fungus) is a perennial wood-decay basidiomycete found in Europe, Asia, Africa and North America.

items.name: Spaurán tindi
items.text: Tinder pouch: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Tinder is easily combustible material used to start a fire.

items.name: Slaut iaskuirechta
items.text: Fishing rod: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). A fishing rod  or fishing pole is a long, thin rod used by anglers to catch fish by manipulating a line ending in a hook (formerly known as an angle, hence the term "angling").

items.name: Die-iask
items.text: Fish hook: earliest widespread use c. 40000 BC (Worldwide). A fish hook or fishhook, formerly also called an angle (from Old English angol and Proto-Germanic *angulaz), is a hook used to catch fish either by piercing and embedding onto the inside of the fish mouth (angling) or, more rarely, by impaling and snagging the external fish body.

items.name: Líoun iaskuirechta
items.text: Fishing net: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A fishing net or fish net is a net used for fishing.

items.name: Gaisti éisk
items.text: Fish trap: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A fish trap is a trap used for catching fish and other aquatic animals of value.

items.name: Haurpún
items.text: Fishing harpoon: earliest widespread use c. 90000 BC (Africa). A harpoon is a long, spear-like projectile used in fishing, whaling, sealing, and other hunting to shoot, kill, and capture large fish such as sharks or marine mammals such as seals, sea cows, and whales.

items.name: Pold homuir
items.text: Lobster pot: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A lobster trap or lobster pot is a portable trap that traps lobsters or crayfish and is used in lobster fishing.

items.name: Bróu láimi
items.text: Saddle quern: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A quern-stone is a stone tool for hand-grinding a wide variety of materials, especially for various types of grains.

items.name: Kloch mhoilind
items.text: Millstone: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). Millstones or mill stones are stones used in gristmills, used for triturating, crushing or, more specifically, grinding wheat or other grains.

items.name: Mrtau augus pieslí
items.text: Mortar and pestle: earliest widespread use c. 35000 BC (Worldwide). A mortar and pestle is a set of two simple tools used to prepare ingredients or substances by crushing and grinding them into a fine paste or powder in the kitchen, laboratory, and pharmacy.

items.name: Raka triumaiti
items.text: Drying rack: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Food drying is a method of food preservation in which food is dried (dehydrated or desiccated).

items.name: Boidéul kanála
items.text: Mason jar: earliest widespread use 1858 (USA). A Mason jar, also known as a canning jar, preserves jar or fruit jar, is a glass jar used in home canning to preserve food.

items.name: Boidéul kaemnaiti
items.text: Preserving jar: earliest widespread use 1810 (France). Canning is a method of food preservation in which food is processed and sealed in an airtight container (jars like Mason jars, and steel and tin cans).

items.name: Kroguld biutáildi
items.text: Fermentation crock: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). In food processing, fermentation is the conversion of carbohydrates to alcohol or organic acids using microorganisms—yeasts or bacteria—without an oxidizing agent being used in the reaction.

items.name: Roldadán
items.text: Rolling pin: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A rolling pin is a cylindrical food preparation utensil used to shape and flatten dough.

items.name: Rota taesráin
items.text: Pastry wheel: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A pastry wheel, also known as a pastry jigger or jagging wheel, is a kitchen tool which is used to cut pastry and other doughs.

items.name: Gierrta briuska
items.text: Cookie cutter: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A cookie cutter (also known as a biscuit cutter outside the US) is a tool for cutting cookie dough into a particular shape, by pressing a shaped blade down into the dough.

items.name: Brúchánu briuska
items.text: Cookie press: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A cookie press, also known as a cookie gun, is a device for making pressed cookies such as spritz cookies.

items.name: Málau píoupála
items.text: Piping bag: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). A pastry bag (or piping bag in the Commonwealth) is an often cone- or triangular-shaped bag made from cloth, paper, plastic, or the intestinal lining of a lamb, that is squeezed by hand to pipe semi-solid foods by pressing them through a narrow opening at one end often fitted with a shaped nozzle, f

items.name: Skríobtóir taes
items.text: Bench scraper: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A kitchen scraper is a kitchen implement made of metal, plastics (such as polyethylene, nylon, or polypropylene), wood, rubber or silicone rubber.

items.name: Tráta taesráin
items.text: Dough trough: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). In cooking (and more specifically baking), kneading is a process in the making of bread dough, used to mix the ingredients and add strength and stiffness to the final product.

items.name: Kiseán taesráin
items.text: Banneton: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Proofing (North American) or proving (British and Australasia) is a step in the preparation of yeast bread and other baked goods in which the dough is allowed to rest and rise a final time before baking.

items.name: Skian auráin
items.text: Bread lame: earliest widespread use 1900s (France). A lame (, from French lame, derived from Latin lāmina, meaning blade) is a double-sided blade that is used to slash the tops of bread loaves before baking.

items.name: Babla mieskta
items.text: Mixing bowl: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A mixing bowl is a bowl used for mixing of ingredients.

items.name: Koisel
items.text: Colander: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A colander or cullender is a kitchen utensil perforated with holes used to strain foods such as pasta or to rinse vegetables.

items.name: Kriatur
items.text: Sieve: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A sieve (), fine mesh strainer, or sift is a tool used for separating wanted elements from unwanted material or for controlling the particle size distribution of a sample, using a screen such as a woven mesh or net or perforated sheet material.

items.name: Éaudach káisi
items.text: Cheesecloth: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Cheesecloth is a loose-woven gauze-like carded cotton cloth used primarily in cheesemaking and cooking.

items.name: Kataeir admaid
items.text: Wooden chair: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A chair (/t͡ʃɛɚ/ ) is a type of seat, typically designed for one person and consisting of one or more legs, a flat or slightly angled seat, and a back rest.

items.name: Stólu tríu chous
items.text: Three-legged stool: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Stool may refer to:

items.name: Binsi
items.text: Bench: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A bench is a long seat on which several people may sit at the same time.

items.name: Bourd admaid
items.text: Wooden table: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A table is a piece of furniture with a raised flat top and is supported most commonly by 1 to 4 legs (although some can have more).

items.name: Lieba
items.text: Bed frame: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A bed is a piece of furniture that is used as a place to sleep, rest, and relax.

items.name: Kliabán
items.text: Cradle: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Cradle or Cradles may refer to:

items.name: Seilfi liebur
items.text: Bookshelf: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A bookcase also called a bookshelf, is a piece of furniture with horizontal shelves, often in a cabinet, used to store books or other printed materials.

items.name: Kófra
items.text: Cupboard: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A cupboard is a piece of furniture for enclosing dishware or grocery items that are stored in a home.

items.name: Prius éaudaí
items.text: Wardrobe: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A wardrobe, also called armoire or almirah, is a piece of standing furniture used for storing clothes.

items.name: Kasúr krúka
items.text: Claw hammer: earliest widespread use c. 1st c. AD (Rome). A claw hammer is a hammer primarily used in carpentry for driving nails into or pulling them from wood.

items.name: Kasúr móru
items.text: Sledgehammer: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A sledgehammer or sledge is a tool with a flat, massive, often metal head, attached to a long wooden or solid handle.

items.name: Kasúr admaid
items.text: Mallet: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A mallet is a tool used for imparting force on another object, often made of rubber or sometimes wood, that is smaller than a maul or beetle, and usually has a relatively large head.

items.name: Gléaus griemaiti
items.text: Bench vise: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A vise or vice (British English) is a mechanical apparatus used to secure an object to allow work to be performed on it.

items.name: Griemeig
items.text: Pincers: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Pincer may refer to:

items.name: Spanur
items.text: Spanner wrench: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A wrench or spanner  is a tool used to provide grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to turn objects—usually rotary fasteners, such as nuts and bolts—or keep them from turning.

items.name: Spanur inatraiti
items.text: Monkey wrench: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). An adjustable spanner (UK), also called a shifting spanner or shifter (Australia and New Zealand) or adjustable wrench (US and Canada), is any of various styles of spanner (wrench) with a movable jaw, allowing it to be used with different sizes of fastener head (nut, bolt, etc.) rather than just one

items.name: Skriúiri
items.text: Screwdriver: earliest widespread use 1400s (Europe). A  screwdriver is a tool, manual or powered, used for turning screws.

items.name: Krobur
items.text: Crowbar: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A crowbar is a lever consisting of a metal bar with a single curved end and flattened points, used to force two objects apart or gain mechanical advantage in lifting; often the curved end has a notch for removing nails.

items.name: Puilaí
items.text: Pulley: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Mesopotamia). A pulley is a wheel on an axle or shaft enabling a taut cable or belt passing over the wheel to move and change direction, or transfer power between itself and a shaft.

items.name: Blok augus taka
items.text: Block and tackle: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A block and tackle, purchase, or only tackle is a system of two or more pulleys with a rope or cable threaded between them, used to provide tension and lift heavy loads.

items.name: Krand tarruingti
items.text: Winch: earliest widespread use Ancient (Greece). A winch is a mechanical device that is used to pull in (wind up) or let out (wind out) or otherwise adjust the tension of a rope or wire rope (also called "cable" or "wire cable").

items.name: Krand kasta
items.text: Windlass: earliest widespread use Ancient (Greece). The windlass  is a type of horizontal winch used to move heavy weights, featuring a cylinder (barrel) operated by a crank to wind a rope.

items.name: Kaibisten
items.text: Capstan: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A capstan is a vertical-axled rotating machine developed for use on sailing ships to multiply the pulling force of sailors when hauling ropes, cables, and hawsers.

items.name: Luomán
items.text: Lever: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A lever is a simple machine consisting of a beam or rigid rod pivoted at a fixed hinge or fulcrum.

items.name: Dréimiri
items.text: Ladder: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A ladder is a vertical or inclined set of rungs or steps commonly used for climbing or descending.

items.name: Krúka graupnéil
items.text: Grappling hook: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A grappling hook, or grapnel, is a drag-looking device intended for grappling onto something.

items.name: Kiengul iaruind
items.text: Iron shackle: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A shackle (or shacklebolt), also known as a gyve, is a U-shaped piece of metal secured with a clevis pin or bolt across the opening, or a hinged metal loop secured with a quick-release locking pin mechanism.

items.name: Slabra iaruind
items.text: Iron chain: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A chain is a serial assembly of connected links typically made of metal, with an overall character similar to that of a rope in that it is flexible and curved in compression, but linear, rigid, and load-bearing in tension.

items.name: Tairni iaruind
items.text: Iron nail: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). In woodworking and construction, a nail is a small object made of metal (or wood, called a tree nail or "trunnel") which is used as a fastener, as a peg to hang something, or sometimes as a decoration.

items.name: Skriú admaid
items.text: Wood screw: earliest widespread use 1500s (Europe). A screw is an externally helical threaded fastener capable of being tightened or released by a twisting force (torque) to the head.

items.name: Boulta augus knó
items.text: Nut and bolt: earliest widespread use 1500s (Europe). A bolt is an externally helical threaded fastener capable of being tightened or released by a twisting force (torque) to a matching nut.

items.name: Pouta ungad
items.text: Grease pot: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Grease is a solid or semisolid lubricant formed as a dispersion of thickening agents in a liquid lubricant.

items.name: Kanda oula
items.text: Oil can: earliest widespread use 1800s (Worldwide). An oil can (oilcan or oiler) is a can that holds oil (usually motor oil) for lubricating machines.

items.name: Gunda ungaid
items.text: Grease gun: earliest widespread use 1900s (Worldwide). A grease gun is a common workshop and garage tool used for lubrication.

items.name: Kaidéul láimi
items.text: Hand pump: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (Greece). A pump is a device that moves fluids (liquids or gases), or sometimes slurries, by mechanical action, typically converted from electrical energy into hydraulic or pneumatic energy.

items.name: Píoubán gloini
items.text: Blowpipe: earliest widespread use c. 50 BC (Levant). Glassblowing is a glassforming technique that involves inflating molten glass into a bubble (or parison) with the aid of a blowpipe (or blow tube).

items.name: Iarund tiesa
items.text: Sad iron: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A clothes iron, also known as a flatiron, smoothing iron, dry iron, steam iron, and simply iron, is a small appliance that, when heated, is used to press clothes to remove wrinkles and unwanted creases.

items.name: Glaus
items.text: Padlock: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (Eurasia). Padlocks are portable locks with a shackle that may be passed through an opening (such as a chain link, or hasp staple) to prevent use, theft, vandalism or harm.

items.name: Eochuir
items.text: Door key: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). A lock is a mechanical or electronic fastening device that is released by a physical object (such as a key, keycard, fingerprint, RFID card, security token or coin), by supplying secret information (such as a number or letter permutation or password), by a combination thereof, or it may only be able

items.name: Glaus biuráin
items.text: Pin tumbler lock: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). The pin tumbler lock, also known as the Yale lock (after Linus Yale Jr) is a lock mechanism that uses a series of spring-loaded pins of varying lengths to prevent the lock from opening without the correct key.

items.name: Glaus luomáin
items.text: Lever lock: earliest widespread use 1778 (England). A lever tumbler lock is a type of lock whose mechanism uses a set of levers to prevent the bolt from moving in the lock.

items.name: Lúbu dourais
items.text: Door hinge: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A hinge is a mechanical bearing that connects two solid objects, typically allowing only a limited angle of rotation between them.

items.name: Boikéad admaid
items.text: Wooden bucket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A bucket is typically a watertight, vertical cylinder or truncated cone or square, with an open top and a flat bottom that is attached to a semicircular carrying handle called the bail.

items.name: Boikéad tobuir
items.text: Well bucket and windlass: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A well is an excavation or structure created on the earth by digging, driving, or drilling to access liquid resources, usually water.

items.name: Fiedán tiontaiti
items.text: Funnel: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A funnel is a tube or pipe that is wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, used for guiding liquid or powder into a small opening.

items.name: Ladur móru
items.text: Dipper: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A ladle is a large, deep spoon, often used in the preparation and serving of soup, stew, or other foods.

items.name: Andursaí
items.text: Andiron: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). An andiron,  firedog, fire-dog, fire dog,  iron-dog, or chenet is a bracket support, normally one of a pair, on which logs are laid for burning in an open fireplace, so that air may circulate under the firewood, allowing better burning and less smoke.

items.name: Skuob
items.text: Besom broom: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A broom (), also known as a broomstick, is a cleaning tool, consisting of usually stiff fibers (often made of materials such as plastic, glued hair, or corn husks) attached to, and roughly parallel to, a cylindrical handle, the broomstick.

items.name: Liatróid lausta
items.text: Dustpan: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A dustpan, the small version of which is also known as a "hearth brush and shovel” (from its use of cleaning the fireplace hearth), is a cleaning utensil.

items.name: Maupa
items.text: Mop: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A mop (such as a floor mop) is a mass or bundle of coarse strings or yarn, etc., or a piece of cloth, sponge or other absorbent material, attached to a pole or stick.

items.name: Skuob skuobta
items.text: Scrub brush: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A brush is a common tool with bristles, wire, or other filaments.

items.name: Báiesín nig
items.text: Wash basin: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Basin may refer to:

items.name: Klár nig
items.text: Washboard: earliest widespread use 1797 (USA). Washboard may refer to:

items.name: Toubán nig
items.text: Wash tub: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe).

items.name: Maidm nig
items.text: Laundry beetle: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Laundry is the washing of clothing and other textiles, and, more broadly, their drying and ironing as well.

items.name: Mangul láimi
items.text: Hand mangle: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A mangle is a mechanical laundry aid consisting of two rollers in a sturdy frame, connected by cogs and, in its home version, powered by a hand crank or by electricity.

items.name: Pionda éadeig
items.text: Clothes peg: earliest widespread use 1800s (USA). A clothespin (US English) or clothes peg (UK English), also spelled "clothes pin"  is a fastener used to hang up clothes for drying, usually on a clothes line.

items.name: Líni éadeig
items.text: Clothes line: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A clothes line, also spelled clothesline, also known as a wash line, is a device for hanging clothes on for the purpose of drying or airing out the articles.

items.name: Galdúnach
items.text: Soap bar: earliest widespread use c. 2800 BC (Babylon). Soap is a salt of a fatty acid (sometimes other carboxylic acids) used for cleaning and lubricating products as well as other applications.

items.name: Póiet oíchi
items.text: Chamber pot: earliest widespread use Ancient (Greece). A chamber pot is a portable toilet, meant for nocturnal use in the bedroom.

items.name: Tiesuiri liepa
items.text: Bed warming pan: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bed warmer or warming pan was a common household item in countries with cold winters, especially in Europe.

items.name: Boidéul oiski tie
items.text: Hot water bottle: earliest widespread use 1903 (Europe). A hot-water bottle is a bottle filled with hot water and sealed with a stopper, used to provide warmth, typically while in bed, but also for the application of heat to a specific part of the body.

items.name: Lúbauch láimi
items.text: Hand fan: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A handheld fan, or simply hand fan, is a broad, flat surface that is waved back and forth to create an airflow.

items.name: Skád báiestí
items.text: Umbrella: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (China). An umbrella (parasol or rarely parapluie) is a folding canopy supported by wooden or metal ribs that is mounted on a wooden, metal, or plastic pole.

items.name: Skátán láimi kré-uma
items.text: Bronze hand mirror: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Egypt). A mirror, also known as a looking glass, is an object that reflects an image.

items.name: Fiakla
items.text: Comb: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A comb is a tool consisting of a shaft that holds a row of teeth for pulling through the hair to clean, untangle, or style it.

items.name: Skuob gruoigi
items.text: Hairbrush: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A hairbrush is a brush with rigid (hard or inflexible) or light and soft spokes used in hair care for smoothing, styling, and detangling human hair, or for grooming an animal's fur.

items.name: Rásúru
items.text: Straight razor: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). A razor is a bladed tool primarily used in the removal of body hair through the act of shaving.

items.name: Biuráin
items.text: Tweezers: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). Tweezers are small hand tools used for grasping objects too small to be easily handled with the human fingers.

items.name: Skuob fiakla
items.text: Toothbrush: earliest widespread use 1498 (China). A toothbrush is a special type of brush used to clean the teeth, gums, and tongue.

items.name: Gierrtóirí ingni
items.text: Nail clippers: earliest widespread use 1870s (USA). A nail clipper (also called nail clippers, a nail trimmer, a nail cutter or nipper type) is a hand tool used to trim nails and hangnails.

items.name: Sluosaid tini
items.text: Fire shovel: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A fireplace or hearth is a structure made of brick, stone or metal designed to contain a fire.

items.name: Boska guoil
items.text: Coal scuttle: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A coal scuttle, sometimes spelled coalscuttle and also called a hod, "coal bucket", or "coal pail", is a bucket-like container for holding a small, intermediate supply of coal convenient to an indoor coal-fired stove or heater.

items.name: Stób iaruind
items.text: Cast iron stove: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A stove or range is an appliance or construction that generates heat inside or atop the device using an energy source.

items.name: Stób boulgach
items.text: Pot-bellied stove: earliest widespread use 1800s (USA). A potbelly stove is a cast-iron, coal-burning or wood-burning stove that is cylindrical with a bulge in the middle.

items.name: Lieba thiesaiti
items.text: Kang bed-stove: earliest widespread use Neolithic (China). The kang (Chinese: 炕; pinyin: kàng; Manchu: ᠨᠠᡥᠠᠨ nahan, Kazakh: кән) is a traditional heated platform, 2 metres or more long, used for general living, working, entertaining and sleeping in the northern part of China, where the winter climate is cold.

items.name: Brausúr guoil
items.text: Brazier: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A brazier () is a container used to burn charcoal or other solid fuel for cooking, heating, and/or rituals.

items.name: Táblau faei phloid
items.text: Kotatsu: earliest widespread use 1400s (Japan). A kotatsu (Japanese: 炬燵 or こたつ) is a low, wooden table frame covered by a futon, or heavy blanket, upon which a table top sits.

items.name: Klog láimi
items.text: Hand bell: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (China). A handbell is a bell designed to be rung by hand.

items.name: Goung
items.text: Gong: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (East Asia). A gong is a percussion instrument originating from Southeast Asia, and used widely in Southeast Asian and East Asian musical traditions.

items.name: Ribi
items.text: Snare trap: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Animal trapping, or simply trapping or ginning, is the use of a device to remotely catch and often kill an animal.

items.name: Sub
items.text: Awl: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). Awl may refer to:

items.name: Bíouma kraikend
items.text: Fleshing beam: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Tanning, or hide tanning, is the process of treating skins and hides of animals to produce leather.

items.name: Láisti brógau
items.text: Cobbler's last: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A last is a mechanical form used by shoemakers and cordwainers in the manufacture and repair of shoes.

items.name: Skian chraikend
items.text: Skinning knife: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). The skinner knife or skinning knife is a professional tool for a skinner.

items.name: Laumpa oula krèada
items.text: Clay oil lamp: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). An oil lamp is a lamp used to produce light continuously for a period of time using an oil-based fuel source.

items.name: Koindel
items.text: Tallow candle: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (China). A candle is an ignitable wick embedded in wax, or another flammable solid substance such as tallow, that provides light, and in some cases, a fragrance.

items.name: Koindel luochra
items.text: Rushlight: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A rushlight is a type of candle or miniature torch formed by soaking the dried pith of the rush plant in fat or grease.

items.name: Koindleoir
items.text: Candlestick: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A candlestick (or candleholder) is a device used to hold a candle upright in place.

items.name: Koindlebra
items.text: Candelabra: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A candelabrum (pl.

items.name: Lóchrand adurk
items.text: Horn lantern: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A lantern is a source of lighting, often portable.

items.name: Lóchrand stoirmi
items.text: Hurricane lantern: earliest widespread use 1860s (USA). A kerosene lamp (also known as a paraffin lamp in some countries) is a type of lighting device that uses kerosene as a fuel.

items.name: Tóirsi piki
items.text: Pitch torch: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A torch is a stick with combustible material at one end which can be used as a light source or to set something on fire.

items.name: Laumpa simléura
items.text: Argand lamp: earliest widespread use 1780 (Switzerland). The Argand lamp is a type of oil lamp invented in 1780 by Aimé Argand.

items.name: Múchtóier koindel
items.text: Candle snuffer: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A candle snuffer, candle extinguisher, or douter is an instrument used to extinguish burning candles, consisting of a small cone at the end of a handle.

items.name: Piuk
items.text: Pitching tool: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Stonemasonry, also called stonework or stonecraft, is the creation of buildings, structures, and sculpture using stone as the primary material.

items.name: Múnlau bríkí
items.text: Brick mould: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Mesopotamia). A brick is a type of building material used to build walls, pavements, and other elements in masonry construction.

items.name: Umur aeil
items.text: Mortar tub: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). Mortar  is a workable paste which hardens to bind building blocks such as stones, bricks, and concrete masonry units, to fill and seal the irregular gaps between them, spread the weight of them evenly, and sometimes to add decorative colours or patterns to masonry walls.

items.name: Tomaseoir teibi
items.text: Tape measure: earliest widespread use 1829 (Britain). A tape measure or measuring tape is a long, flexible ruler used to measure length or distance.

items.name: Rialóiri
items.text: Ruler: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Indus). A ruler is an instrument used to make length measurements, whereby a length is read from a series of markings called "rules" along an edge of the device.

items.name: Kiernóg tomais
items.text: Set square: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A set square or triangle (American English) is an object used in engineering and technical drawing, with the aim of providing a straightedge at a right angle or other particular planar angle to a baseline.

items.name: Kiernóg thriaili
items.text: Try square: earliest widespread use Ancient (Egypt). A square is a tool used for marking and referencing a 90° angle, though mitre squares are used for 45° angles.

items.name: Mieá skátánach
items.text: Plumb bob: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Egypt). A plumb bob, plumb bob level, or plummet, is a weight, usually with a pointed tip on the bottom, suspended from a string and used as a vertical direction as a reference line, or plumb-line.

items.name: Leibéul spiurad
items.text: Spirit level: earliest widespread use 1661 (France). A spirit level, bubble level, or simply a level, is an instrument designed to indicate whether a surface is horizontal (level) or vertical (plumb).

items.name: Líni chailk
items.text: Chalk line: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A chalk line or chalk box is a tool for marking long, straight lines on relatively flat surfaces, much further than is practical by hand or with a straightedge.

items.name: Skoltuiri
items.text: Dividers: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Calipers or callipers are an instrument used to measure the linear dimensions of an object or hole; namely, the length, width, thickness, diameter or depth of an object or hole.

items.name: Gnoumón gréini
items.text: Sundial: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). A sundial is a horological device that tells the time of day (referred to as civil time in modern usage) when direct sunlight shines by the apparent position of the Sun in the sky.

items.name: Uoiníocht ghainim
items.text: Hourglass: earliest widespread use c. 1300 (Europe). An hourglass (or sandglass, sand timer, or sand clock) is a device used to measure the passage of time.

items.name: Klog oiski
items.text: Water clock: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). Clepsydra may refer to:  Clepsydra, an alternative name for a water clock.

items.name: Mieá kotrumaiti
items.text: Balance scale: earliest widespread use c. 2400 BC (Indus). A scale or balance is a device used to measure weight or mass.

items.name: Mieá lám
items.text: Steelyard balance: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A steelyard balance, steelyard, or stilyard is a straight-beam balance with arms of unequal length.

items.name: Mieá spriongachu
items.text: Spring scale: earliest widespread use 1770 (Britain). A spring scale, also known as a spring balance or newton meter, is a type of mechanical force gauge or weighing scale.

items.name: Kompás meignéadach
items.text: Magnetic compass: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (China). A compass is a device that shows the cardinal directions used for navigation and geographic orientation.

items.name: Astrulab
items.text: Astrolabe: earliest widespread use c. 200 BC (Greece). An astrolabe (Ancient Greek: ἀστρολάβος, romanized: astrolábos, lit. 'star-taker'; Arabic: ٱلأَسْطُرلاب, romanized: al-Asṭurlāb; Persian: ستاره‌یاب, romanized: Setāreyāb) is an astronomical instrument dating to ancient times.

items.name: Siestán
items.text: Sextant: earliest widespread use 1731 (Britain). A sextant is a doubly reflecting navigation instrument that measures the angular distance between two visible objects.

items.name: Teirmiméadur mierkuir
items.text: Mercury thermometer: earliest widespread use 1714 (Germany). A thermometer is a device that measures temperature (the hotness or coldness of an object).

items.name: Aerbrú-mhéadur
items.text: Barometer: earliest widespread use 1643 (Italy). A barometer is a scientific instrument that is used to measure air pressure.

items.name: Riaili shliemnáin
items.text: Slide rule: earliest widespread use 1622 (England). A slide rule is a hand-operated mechanical calculator consisting of slidable rulers for conducting mathematical operations such as multiplication, division, exponents, roots, logarithms, and trigonometry.

items.name: Priuk lárnauch
items.text: Centre punch: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Eurasia). A punch is a tool used to indent or create a hole through a hard surface.

items.name: Sáb miutuil
items.text: Hacksaw: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A hacksaw is a fine-toothed saw, originally and mainly made for cutting metal.

items.name: Komad
items.text: File: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). A file is a tool used to remove fine amounts of material from a workpiece.

items.name: Toungs gaba
items.text: Smith's tongs: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Tongs are a type of tool used to grip and lift objects, often too hot to hold, instead of holding them with the hands.

items.name: Indeoin
items.text: Anvil: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). An anvil is a metalworking tool consisting of a large block of metal (usually forged or cast steel), with a flattened top surface, upon which another object is struck (or "worked").

items.name: Blok krutaiti
items.text: Swage block: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A swage block (or swager block) is a large, heavy block of cast iron or steel used in smithing, with variously sized holes in its face and usually with forms on the sides.

items.name: Bolguiri
items.text: Bellows: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Eurasia). Bellows are a device constructed to expel a controlled blast of air.

items.name: Plieúrs
items.text: Pliers: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Pliers are a hand tool used to hold objects firmly, possibly developed from tongs used to handle hot metal in Bronze Age Europe.

items.name: Rievéad
items.text: Rivet: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). A rivet is a semi permanent mechanical fastener.

items.name: Kroiskín
items.text: Crucible: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A crucible is a container in which metals or other substances are melted or subjected to very high temperatures.

items.name: Múnlau ingini
items.text: Ingot mould: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). An ingot is a piece of relatively pure material, usually metal, that is cast into a shape suitable for further processing.

items.name: Ladul kaisti
items.text: Casting ladle: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Worldwide). A foundry is a factory that produces metal castings.

items.name: Kasúr dieng
items.text: Cross-peen hammer: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A ball-peen (also ball-pein) or machinist's hammer is a type of peening hammer used in metalworking.

items.name: Kasúr toisli
items.text: Trip hammer: earliest widespread use Han (China). A trip hammer, also known as a tilt hammer or helve hammer, is a massive powered hammer, usually raised by a cam and then released to fall under the force of gravity.

items.name: Plátau tarruingti
items.text: Draw plate: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Wire drawing is a metalworking process used to reduce the cross-section of a wire by pulling the wire through one or more dies.

items.name: Sáb seodórad
items.text: Jeweller's saw: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A piercing saw, also known as a jeweler's saw or jeweler's blade, is a type of saw commonly used in jewelry making on sheet metal.

items.name: Píki
items.text: Pickaxe: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A pickaxe (American spelling: pickax), pick-axe, or pick is a generally T-shaped hand tool used for digging.

items.name: Kasúr karraigi
items.text: Rock hammer: earliest widespread use 1800s (Worldwide). A geologist's hammer, also known as rock hammer, rock pick, geological pick, or geo pick, is a specialized hammer used for splitting and breaking rocks.

items.name: Laumpa mianadórad
items.text: Davy lamp: earliest widespread use 1815 (Britain). The Davy lamp is a safety lamp used in flammable atmospheres, invented in 1815 by Sir Humphry Davy.

items.name: Trieskuir láimi
items.text: Hand-steel drill (jack hammer): earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A jackhammer (pneumatic drill, breaker, demolition hammer or road hammer in Commonwealth English) is a pneumatic or electro-mechanical tool that combines a hammer directly with a chisel.

items.name: Rod potuiri
items.text: Potter's wheel: earliest widespread use c. 3500 BC (Mesopotamia). In pottery, a potter's wheel is a machine used in the shaping (known as throwing) of clay into round ceramic ware.

items.name: Paidili potuiri
items.text: Paddle and anvil: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Pottery is the process and the products of forming vessels and other objects with clay and other raw materials, which are fired at high temperatures to give them a hard and durable form.

items.name: Fournacha
items.text: Updraft kiln: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A kiln is a thermally insulated chamber, a type of oven, that produces temperatures sufficient to complete some process, such as hardening, drying, or chemical changes.

items.name: Kloch faebraiti
items.text: Whetstone: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Whetstone may refer to:

items.name: Kloch ghrinditi
items.text: Grindstone: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A grindstone, also known as grinding stone, is a sharpening stone used for grinding or sharpening ferrous tools, used since ancient times.

items.name: Tuo láimi
items.text: Hand axe: earliest widespread use 1.7 Mya (Africa). A hand axe (or handaxe or  Acheulean hand axe) is a prehistoric stone tool with two faces that is the longest-used tool in human history.

items.name: Skríobadán kraikend
items.text: Hide scraper: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In prehistoric archaeology, scrapers are unifacial tools thought to have been used for hideworking and woodworking.

items.name: Land chloichi
items.text: Flint blade: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In archaeology, a lithic blade is a type of stone tool created during lithic reduction by striking a long narrow flake from a stone core.

items.name: Skian chloichi
items.text: Stone knife: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A knife (pl.: knives; from Old Norse knifr 'knife, dirk') is a tool or weapon with a cutting edge or blade, usually attached to a handle or hilt.

items.name: Kasúr kloichi
items.text: Hammerstone: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). In archaeology, a hammerstone is a hard cobble used to strike off lithic flakes from a lump of tool stone during the process of lithic reduction.

items.name: Amfur
items.text: Amphora: earliest widespread use c. 5000 BC (Mediterranean). An amphora (; Ancient Greek: ἀμφορεύς, romanized: amphoreús; English pl. amphorae or amphoras) is a type of storage and transport jar with a pointed bottom and characteristic shape and size which fit tightly (and therefore safely) against each other in storage rooms and packages, tied together with

items.name: Pites
items.text: Pithos: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Greece). Pithos (, Ancient Greek: πίθος, plural: pithoi πίθοι) is the Greek name of a large storage container.

items.name: Kvievri
items.text: Qvevri: earliest widespread use c. 6000 BC (Georgia). Kvevri or qvevri (Georgian: ქვევრი [ˈkʰvɛvɾi]) - also known as ch'uri  (Georgian: ჭური [ˈtʃʼuɾi]) in Western Georgia - are large earthenware vessels used for the fermentation, storage and aging of traditional Georgian wine.

items.name: Kroguld stórálau kré
items.text: Clay storage jar: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A jar is a rigid, cylindrical, or slightly conical container, typically made of glass, ceramic, or plastic, with a wide mouth or opening that can be closed with a lid, screw cap, lug cap, cork stopper, roll-on cap, crimp-on cap, press-on cap, plastic shrink, heat-sealed lidding film, an inner seal,

items.name: Krúiskín kanópach
items.text: Canopic jar: earliest widespread use c. 2600 BC (Egypt). Canopic jars are funerary vessels that were used by the ancient Egyptians to house embalmed organs that were removed during the mummification process.

items.name: Boidéul gloini
items.text: Glass bottle: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A bottle is a narrow-necked container made of an impermeable material (such as glass, pottery, porcelain, plastic or aluminium) in various shapes and sizes that stores and transports liquids.

items.name: Kiseán
items.text: Woven basket: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A basket is a container that is traditionally constructed from stiff fibers, and can be made from a range of materials, including wood splints, runners, and cane.

items.name: Kiseán sailech
items.text: Wicker basket: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Wicker is a method of weaving used to make products such as furniture and baskets, as well as a descriptor to classify such products.

items.name: Kliab
items.text: Creel: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Creel and Creels can refer to:

items.name: Kiseán lóien
items.text: Hamper: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A hamper refers to one of several related basket-like items.

items.name: Baruildi bieg
items.text: Keg: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A keg is a small cask used for storing liquids.

items.name: Kliab admaid
items.text: Wooden crate: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A crate is a large shipping container, often made of wood, typically used to transport or store large, heavy items.

items.name: Kófra admaid
items.text: Wooden chest: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A chest (also called a coffer or kist) is a type of furniture typically having a rectangular structure with four walls and a removable or hinged lid, often rounded.

items.name: Kófra
items.text: Coffer: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A coffer (or coffering) in  architecture is a series of sunken panels in the shape of a square, rectangle, or octagon in a ceiling, soffit or vault.

items.name: Trunk taistili
items.text: Travel trunk: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A trunk, also known as a travel trunk, is a large cuboid container designed to hold clothes and other personal belongings.

items.name: Málau skoili
items.text: Satchel: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A satchel is a bag with a strap, traditionally used for carrying books.

items.name: Málau kapuild
items.text: Saddlebag: earliest widespread use Ancient (Eurasia). Saddlebags are bags that are attached to saddles.

items.name: Málau drouma
items.text: Backpack: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A backpack, also called knapsack, schoolbag, rucksack, pack, booksack, bookbag, haversack, packsack, or backsack, is in its simplest frameless form, a fabric sack carried on one’s back and secured with two straps that go over the shoulders, and is used to carry goods from one place to another.

items.name: Spaurán
items.text: Coin purse: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A purse or pouch (from the Latin bursa, which in turn, is from the Greek βύρσα, býrsa, oxhide), sometimes called coin purse for clarity, is a small money bag or pouch, made for carrying coins.

items.name: Kanda stáien
items.text: Tin can: earliest widespread use 1810 (England). A steel can, tin can, tin (especially in British English, Australian English, Canadian English and South African English), or can is a  container made of thin metal, for distribution or storage of goods.

items.name: Krúiskín briuska
items.text: Cookie jar: earliest widespread use 1900s (USA). Cookie jars are utilitarian or decorative ceramic or glass jars often found in American and Canadian kitchens.

items.name: Sierrach spíousraí
items.text: Spice jar: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). In the culinary arts, a spice is a seed, fruit, root, bark, or other plant substance primarily used for flavouring or colouring food.

items.name: Boska taed
items.text: Tea caddy: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A tea caddy is a box, jar, canister, or other receptacle used to store tea.

items.name: Boska auráin
items.text: Bread bin: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A breadbox (chiefly American) or a breadbin (chiefly British) is a container for storing bread and other baked goods to keep them fresh.

items.name: Koisneoir oigir
items.text: Icebox: earliest widespread use 1800s (USA). An icebox (also called a cold closet) is a compact, non-mechanical refrigerator which was a common early-twentieth-century kitchen appliance before the development of safely powered refrigeration devices.

items.name: Boska fréamóg
items.text: Root bin: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A root cellar (American and Canadian English), fruit cellar (Mid-Western American English) or earth cellar (British English) is a structure, usually underground or partially underground, used for storage of vegetables, fruits, nuts, or other foods.

items.name: Sáisedán saluind
items.text: Salt cellar: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A salt cellar (also called a salt, salt-box) is an article of tableware for holding and dispensing salt.

items.name: Babla
items.text: Bowl: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A bowl is a typically round dish or container generally used for preparing, serving, storing, or consuming food.

items.name: Plátau
items.text: Plate: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A plate is a broad, mainly flat vessel on which food can be served.

items.name: Plátau admaid
items.text: Trencher: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Trencher may refer to:

items.name: Plátau friestuil
items.text: Serving platter: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Platter may refer to:

items.name: Plátau dindéir
items.text: Porcelain plate: earliest widespread use Tang (China). Porcelain (), also called china, is a ceramic material made by heating raw materials, generally including kaolinite, in a kiln to temperatures between 1,200 and 1,400 °C (2,200 and 2,600 °F).

items.name: Fouchupán
items.text: Saucer: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A saucer is a type of small dishware used to support a cup or a potted plant.

items.name: Muiga
items.text: Mug: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A mug is a type of cup, a drinking vessel usually intended for hot drinks such as coffee, hot chocolate, or tea.

items.name: Kandán
items.text: Tankard: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A tankard is a form of drinkware consisting of a large, roughly cylindrical, drinking cup with a single handle.

items.name: Goubléad
items.text: Goblet: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A chalice (from Latin calix 'cup', taken from the Ancient Greek κύλιξ (kylix) 'cup') is a drinking cup raised on a stem with a foot or base.

items.name: Gloini fíouna
items.text: Wine glass: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A wine glass is a type of glass that is used for drinking or tasting wine.

items.name: Gloini ghierr
items.text: Tumbler: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A tumbler is a flat-floored beverage container usually made of plastic, glass or stainless steel.

items.name: Gloini dheochunda bhieg
