items.text: Shot glass: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A shot glass is a glass originally designed to hold or measure spirits or liquor, which is either imbibed straight from the glass ("a shot") or poured into a cocktail ("a drink").

items.name: Adurk óiel
items.text: Drinking horn: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Eurasia). A drinking horn is the horn of a bovid or antler of an ungulate used as a drinking vessel.

items.name: Kupán taed
items.text: Tea bowl: earliest widespread use Tang (China). Tea bowl may refer to:

items.name: Kupán taed sínéisech
items.text: Gaiwan: earliest widespread use Ming (China). A gaiwan (simplified Chinese: 盖碗; traditional Chinese: 蓋碗; ) or zhong (盅) is a Chinese lidded bowl without a handle, used for the infusion of tea leaves and the consumption of tea.

items.name: Kupán saki
items.text: Sake cup: earliest widespread use Japan (Japan). A sake set (酒器, shuki) consists of the flask and cups used to serve sake.

items.name: Krúiskín
items.text: Pitcher: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). In American English, a pitcher is a container with a handle and a spout, used for storing and pouring liquids.

items.name: Karafa
items.text: Carafe: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A carafe () is a glass container with a flared lip used for serving liquids, especially wine and coffee.

items.name: Dikuntóir
items.text: Decanter: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A decanter is a vessel that is used to hold the decantation of a liquid (such as wine) which may contain sediment.

items.name: Saikín fíouna
items.text: Wineskin: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A wine bottle is a bottle, generally a glass bottle, that is used for holding wine.

items.name: Flask taistili
items.text: Pilgrim flask: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Flask may refer to:

items.name: Boidéul kuocha
items.text: Gourd canteen: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Calabash (; Lagenaria siceraria) is a vine in the family Cucurbitaceae which is grown for its fruit.

items.name: Kanda
items.text: Canteen: earliest widespread use 1800s (Worldwide). Canteen most often refers to:  Canteen (bottle), a water container Cafeteria, a type of food service location within an institution in which there is little or no waiting staff table service A complete set of cutlery comprising knives, forks, and spoons, usually sufficient for several place-settings

items.name: Flask insliti
items.text: Vacuum flask: earliest widespread use 1892 (Britain). A vacuum flask (also known as a Dewar flask, Dewar bottle or thermos) is an insulating storage vessel that slows the rate at which its contents change in temperature.

items.name: Babla punuinsi
items.text: Punch bowl: earliest widespread use 1600s (India). A punch bowl or punchbowl is a bowl, often large and wide, for serving mixed drinks such as hippocras, punch or mulled wine, with a ladle.

items.name: Túierín anraid
items.text: Soup tureen: earliest widespread use 1700s (France). A tureen is a serving dish for foods such as soups or stews, often shaped as a broad, deep, oval vessel with fixed handles and a low domed cover with a knob or handle.

items.name: Bádu grauvy
items.text: Gravy boat: earliest widespread use 1700s (France). A sauce boat, gravy boat, or saucière is a low jug or pitcher with a handle in which sauce or gravy is served.

items.name: Miasu imi
items.text: Butter dish: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A butter dish is defined as "a usually round or rectangular dish often with a drainer and a cover for holding butter at table".

items.name: Siestán káka
items.text: Cake stand: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A cake stand is a type of tableware used for serving cake and other pastries, or a type of kitchen equipment used for holding cakes while they are decorated.

items.name: Kupán oibi
items.text: Egg cup: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). An egg cup or eggcup, sometimes called an egg server, is an item of tableware used for serving and holding boiled eggs within their shell.

items.name: Naipkín
items.text: Napkin: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A napkin, serviette or face towelette is a square of cloth or paper tissue used at the table for wiping of the mouth and fingers while eating.

items.name: Éaudach boirdi
items.text: Tablecloth: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A tablecloth is a cloth used to cover a table.

items.name: Mauta boirdi
items.text: Placemat: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A placemat or table mat is a covering or pad designating an individual place setting, unlike the larger tablecloth that covers the entire surface.

items.name: Tráidiri
items.text: Serving tray: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A tray is a shallow platform designed for the carrying of items.

items.name: Táblau kasta
items.text: Lazy Susan: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A lazy Susan is a turntable (rotating tray) placed on a table or countertop to aid in distributing food.

items.name: Biurán fiakla
items.text: Toothpick: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A toothpick is a small thin stick of wood, plastic, bamboo, metal, bone or other substance with at least one and sometimes two pointed ends to insert between teeth to remove detritus, usually after a meal.

items.name: Toild snáta
items.text: Drop spindle: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A spindle is a straight spike, usually made from wood, used for spinning, twisting fibers such as wool, flax, hemp, and cotton into yarn.

items.name: Kuoildi snáta
items.text: Distaff: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A distaff (, , also called a rock) is a tool used in spinning.

items.name: Rod snáta
items.text: Spinning wheel: earliest widespread use c. 1000 (India). A spinning wheel is a device for spinning thread or yarn from fibres.

items.name: Kíor olda
items.text: Wool comb: earliest widespread use Iron Age (Europe). Combing is a method for preparing carded fibre for spinning.

items.name: Kardunda láimi
items.text: Hand cards: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). In textile production, carding is a mechanical process that disentangles, cleans and intermixes fibres to produce a continuous web or sliver suitable for subsequent processing.

items.name: Kuoildi faldaí
items.text: Niddy-noddy: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A niddy-noddy is a tool used to make skeins from yarn.

items.name: Fíodmagg mieáchun-bhrietnaiti
items.text: Warp-weighted loom: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Europe). The warp-weighted loom is a simple and ancient form of loom in which the warp yarns hang freely from a bar, which is supported by upright poles which can be placed at a convenient slant against a wall.

items.name: Fíodmagg drouma
items.text: Backstrap loom: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Americas). A loom is a device used to weave cloth and tapestry.

items.name: Fier fíodóirechta
items.text: Weaving shuttle: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A shuttle is a tool designed to neatly and compactly store a holder that carries the thread of the weft yarn while weaving with a loom.

items.name: Fier eitilti
items.text: Flying shuttle: earliest widespread use 1733 (England). The flying shuttle or fly shuttle is a type of weaving shuttle.

items.name: Sienaí snáta
items.text: Spinning jenny: earliest widespread use 1764 (England). The spinning jenny is a multi-spindle spinning frame, and was one of the key developments in the industrialisation of textile manufacturing during the early Industrial Revolution.

items.name: Snátaid
items.text: Sewing needle: earliest widespread use c. 50000 BC (Siberia). A sewing needle, used for hand-sewing, is a long slender tool with a pointed tip at one end and a hole (or eye) to hold the sewing thread.

items.name: Snátaid chnáma
items.text: Bone needle: earliest widespread use c. 50000 BC (Worldwide). Needle or Needles may refer to:

items.name: Méarchosuint
items.text: Thimble: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A thimble is a small pitted cup worn on the finger that protects it from being pricked or poked by a needle while sewing.

items.name: Indelra fueigti
items.text: Sewing machine: earliest widespread use 1790 (England). A sewing machine is a machine used to sew fabric and materials together with thread.

items.name: Siusúr
items.text: Scissors: earliest widespread use c. 1500 BC (Egypt). Scissors or shears are hand-operated cutting tools that consist of a pair of pivoting blades whose sharpened edges slide firmly against and past each other when the handles (shank) on the opposite side of the pivot are squeezed shut.

items.name: Snátaidí figti
items.text: Knitting needles: earliest widespread use c. 1000 (Egypt). A knitting needle or knitting pin is a tool in hand-knitting to produce knitted fabrics.

items.name: Krúka krochadóirechta
items.text: Crochet hook: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A crochet hook is a tool used to create loops in thread or yarn and to interlock them into crochet stitches.

items.name: Frámau bróidnéirechta
items.text: Embroidery hoop: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Embroidery hoops and frames are tools used to keep fabric taut while working embroidery or other forms of needlework.

items.name: Indeld tautála
items.text: Tatting shuttle: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). Tatting is a technique for handcrafting a particularly durable lace from a series of knots and loops.

items.name: Umur dataiti
items.text: Dye vat: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). Dyeing is the application of dyes or pigments on textile materials such as fibers, yarns, and fabrics with the goal of achieving color with desired color fastness.

items.name: Maidéul buolta
items.text: Fulling stocks: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). Fulling, also known as tucking or walking (Scots: waukin, hence often spelt waulking in Scottish English), is a step in woollen clothmaking which involves the cleansing of woven cloth (particularly wool) to eliminate (lanolin) oils, dirt, and other impurities, and to make it shrink by friction and p

items.name: Skian chistini
items.text: Kitchen knife: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A kitchen knife is any knife that is intended to be used in food preparation, as opposed to a table knife used when eating, as part of a set of cutlery.

items.name: Skian chókairi
items.text: Chef's knife: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). A chef's knife, also known as a cook's knife, is a medium to large sized generalist kitchen knife used in food preparation.

items.name: Tuo feolad
items.text: Cleaver: earliest widespread use Han dynasty (China). A cleaver is a large knife that varies in its shape but usually resembles a rectangular-bladed tomahawk.

items.name: Skian sauntoku
items.text: Santoku: earliest widespread use 1940s (Japan). The santoku bōchō (Japanese: 三徳包丁; lit. '"three virtues knife" or "three uses knife"') or bunka bōchō (文化包丁) is a general-purpose kitchen knife originating in Japan.

items.name: Skian auráin
items.text: Bread knife: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). Bread knives are used for cutting bread and are one of many kitchen knives used by cooks.

items.name: Skian chnám
items.text: Boning knife: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A boning knife is a type of kitchen knife with a sharp point and a narrow blade.

items.name: Skian fhildéad
items.text: Fillet knife: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A fillet knife (also called a filleting knife) is a kitchen knife used for filleting.

items.name: Skian káisi
items.text: Cheese knife: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A cheese knife is a type of kitchen knife specialized for the cutting of cheese.

items.name: Skian imi
items.text: Butter knife: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). The butter knife is a table knife intended for serving butter and applying it to bread and crackers ("spreading").

items.name: Skian bhoirdi
items.text: Table knife: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A table knife is an item of cutlery with a single cutting edge, and usually a blunt end – part of a table setting.

items.name: Skian lietchiurklach
items.text: Ulu: earliest widespread use c. 2500 BC (Arctic). An ulu (Inuktitut: ᐅᓗ; plural: uluit; sometimes referred to as 'woman's knife') is an all-purpose knife traditionally used by Inuit, Iñupiat, Yupik, and Aleut women.

items.name: Skian lietgelaí
items.text: Mezzaluna: earliest widespread use Medieval (Italy). A mezzaluna ( MET-sə-LOO-nə, Italian: [ˌmɛddzaˈluːna]) is a knife consisting of one or more curved blades with a handle on each end, which is rocked back and forth chopping the ingredients below with each movement.

items.name: Skoránaí glausraí
items.text: Vegetable peeler: earliest widespread use 1947 (Switzerland). A peeler (vegetable scraper) is a kitchen tool,  a distinct type of kitchen knife, consisting of a metal blade with a slot with a sharp edge attached to a handle, used to remove the outer layer (the "skin" or "peel") of some vegetables such as potatoes, broccoli stalks, and carrots, and fruits such

items.name: Grátóier
items.text: Box grater: earliest widespread use 1540s (Italy). A grater, also referred to as a shredder, is a kitchen utensil used to grate or shred foods into fine pieces.

items.name: Grátóier gléinech
items.text: Rasp grater: earliest widespread use 1990s (USA). Microplane is a registered trademark of Grace Manufacturing Inc., a company that makes photo etched steel tools (surform tools) for grating, grinding and sanding.

items.name: Sliemnóir manduilín
items.text: Mandoline slicer: earliest widespread use 1800s (France). A mandoline (US) or mandolin (British) , is a culinary utensil used for slicing and for cutting juliennes; with suitable attachments, it can make crinkle-cuts.

items.name: Fork boirdi
items.text: Table fork: earliest widespread use c. 1000 (Byzantium). In cutlery or kitchenware, a fork (from Latin: furca 'pitchfork') is a utensil, now usually made of metal, whose long handle terminates in a head that branches into several narrow and often slightly curved tines with which one can spear foods either to hold them to cut with a knife or to lift them t

items.name: Spúnógu
items.text: Spoon: earliest widespread use Paleolithic (Worldwide). A spoon (UK: , US:  SPOON) is a utensil consisting of a shallow bowl (also known as a head), oval or round, at the end of a handle.

items.name: Spúnógu anraid
items.text: Soup spoon: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A soup spoon is a type of spoon with a large or rounded bowl, used for consuming soup.

items.name: Spúnógu taed
items.text: Teaspoon: earliest widespread use 1600s (Europe). A teaspoon (tsp.) is a small spoon that can be used to stir a cup of tea or coffee, or as a tool for measuring volume.

items.name: Spúnógu admaid
items.text: Wooden spoon: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A wooden spoon is a utensil commonly used in food preparation.

items.name: Spúnork
items.text: Spork: earliest widespread use 1900s (Worldwide). A spork is a form of cutlery and combination utensil taking the form of a spoon-like scoop with two to four fork-like tines.

items.name: Slauta itecháin
items.text: Chopsticks: earliest widespread use c. 1200 BC (China). Chopsticks are shaped pairs of equal-length sticks that have been used as kitchen and eating utensils in most countries of the Sinosphere for over three millennia.

items.name: Spautúla
items.text: Spatula: earliest widespread use Roman (Worldwide). A spatula is a broad, flat, flexible blade used to mix, spread and lift material, including foods, drugs, plaster and paints.

items.name: Fuoskuilteoir
items.text: Whisk: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A whisk is a cooking utensil which can be used to blend ingredients smooth or to incorporate air into a mixture, in a process known as whisking or whipping.

items.name: Brúieteoir prátauí
items.text: Potato masher: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A potato masher, tater masher, bean masher, pea masher, masher, or crusher is a food preparation utensil used to crush soft food for such dishes as mashed potatoes, apple sauce, or refried beans.

items.name: Brúieteoir prátauí
items.text: Potato ricer: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A potato ricer (also called a ricer) is a kitchen implement used to process potatoes or other food by forcing it through a sheet of small holes, which are typically about the diameter of a grain of rice.

items.name: Brúieteoir gairleoigi
items.text: Garlic press: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A garlic press, also known as a garlic crusher, is a kitchen utensil to crush garlic cloves efficiently by forcing them through a grid of small holes, usually with some type of piston.

items.name: Riemadóir kitrus
items.text: Citrus reamer: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A juicer, also known as a juice extractor, is a tool used to extract juice from fruits, herbs, leafy greens and other types of vegetables in a process called juicing.

items.name: Kranduiri
items.text: Nutcracker: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A nutcracker is a tool designed to open nuts by cracking their shells.

items.name: Kasúr feolad
items.text: Meat tenderizer: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A meat tenderizer or meat pounder is a tool for mechanically tenderizing and flattening slabs of meat.

items.name: Meisín miondaiti feolad
items.text: Meat grinder: earliest widespread use 1845 (Germany). A  meat grinder (also called a "meat mincer" in the UK) is a kitchen appliance for mincing (UK) or grinding (US) meat, fish, vegetables and other foods, raw or cooked.

items.name: Líounadóir puitóg
items.text: Sausage stuffer: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A sausage is a type of meat product usually made from ground meat—often pork, beef, or poultry—along with salt, spices and other flavourings.

items.name: Oskuilteoir kandaí
items.text: Can opener: earliest widespread use 1855 (England). A can opener (North American and Australian English) or tin opener (British English) is a mechanical device used to open metal tin cans.

items.name: Oskuilteoir boidéul
items.text: Bottle opener: earliest widespread use 1892 (USA). A bottle opener or bottle cap opener is a device for removing metal bottle caps from glass bottles.

items.name: Skriú kork
items.text: Corkscrew: earliest widespread use 1630s (England). A corkscrew is a tool for drawing corks from wine bottles and other household bottles that may be sealed with corks.

items.name: Foindedán oibecha
items.text: Hand egg beater: earliest widespread use 1856 (USA). Egg-beater, egg beater, or eggbeater may refer to:

items.name: Miesktóir láimi
items.text: Hand-crank mixer: earliest widespread use 1800s (USA). A mixer (also called a hand mixer or stand mixer depending on the type) is a kitchen device that uses a gear-driven mechanism to rotate a set of "beaters" in a bowl containing the food or liquids to be prepared by mixing them.

items.name: Miesktóir
items.text: Blender: earliest widespread use 1922 (USA). Blender may refer to:

items.name: Moilend biad
items.text: Food mill: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A food mill (also called passatutto, purée sieve, moulinette, mouli légumes, passe-vite, or triturator) is a food preparation utensil for mashing and sieving soft foods invented in Brussels in 1928 by Victor Simon.

items.name: Kasuiri sailéidi
items.text: Salad spinner: earliest widespread use 1970s (France). A salad spinner, also known as a salad tosser, is a kitchen tool used to wash and remove excess water from salad greens.

items.name: Tíousán taed
items.text: Tea infuser: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A tea infuser is a device in which loose, dried tea leaves are placed for steeping or brewing, in a mug or a teapot full of hot water.

items.name: Skaguiri taed
items.text: Tea strainer: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). A tea strainer is a type of strainer that is placed over or in a teacup to catch loose tea leaves.

items.name: Meilteoiri kaifi
items.text: Hand coffee grinder: earliest widespread use 1500s (Ottoman). A burr mill, or burr grinder, is a mill used to grind hard, small food products between two revolving abrasive surfaces separated by a distance usually set by the user.

items.name: Griemuiri siúkra
items.text: Sugar nippers: earliest widespread use 1700s (Europe). Sugar nips are a large pair of pincers with sharp blades, designed to cut sugar from a block.

items.name: Kupán tomais
items.text: Measuring cup: earliest widespread use 1896 (USA). A measuring cup is a kitchen utensil used primarily to measure the volume of liquid or bulk solid cooking ingredients such as flour and sugar, especially for volumes from about 50 mL (approx.

items.name: Spúnógu thomais
items.text: Measuring spoons: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A measuring spoon is a spoon  used to measure an amount of an ingredient, either liquid or dry, when cooking.

items.name: Bourd gierrta
items.text: Cutting board: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A cutting board (or chopping board) is a durable flat surface on which to place material for cutting.

items.name: Bourd búistéura
items.text: Butcher block: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A butcher block or butcher's block is a heavy-duty chopping block, typically laminated or hardwood.

items.name: Adurk
items.text: Adze: earliest widespread use c. 8000 BC (Worldwide). An adze () or adz is an ancient and versatile cutting tool similar to an axe but with the cutting edge perpendicular to the handle rather than parallel.

items.name: Tuo chraind
items.text: Felling axe: earliest widespread use c. 8000 BC (Eurasia). An axe (; sometimes spelled ax in American English; see spelling differences) is an implement that has been used for thousands of years to shape, split, and cut wood, to harvest timber, and as a weapon.

items.name: Tuo lietun
items.text: Broad axe: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (Europe). A broadaxe is a large broad-headed axe.

items.name: Tuo bhieg
items.text: Hatchet: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A hatchet (from the Old French hachete, a diminutive form of hache, 'axe' of Germanic origin) is a single-handed striking tool with a sharp blade on one side used to cut and split wood, and a hammerhead on the other side.

items.name: Maidm
items.text: Maul: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Europe). A maul may refer to any number of large hammers, including:

items.name: Fliesk
items.text: Splitting wedge: earliest widespread use Neolithic (Worldwide). A wedge is a triangular shaped tool, a portable inclined plane, and one of the six simple machines.

items.name: Suáilki
items.text: Chisel: earliest widespread use c. 6000 BC (Worldwide). A chisel is a hand tool with a characteristic wedge-shaped cutting edge on the end of its blade.

items.name: Bierrad kuosach
items.text: Gouge: earliest widespread use Bronze Age (Eurasia). Gouge may refer to:

items.name: Sub admaid
items.text: Bradawl: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bradawl is a woodworking hand tool with a blade similar to that of a straight screwdriver and a handle typically made from wood or plastic.

items.name: Sáb láimi
items.text: Handsaw: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Egypt). In woodworking and carpentry, hand saws, also known as "panel saws", are used to cut pieces of wood into different shapes.

items.name: Sáb frámau
items.text: Frame saw: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A frame saw or sash saw is a type of saw which consists of a relatively narrow and flexible blade held under tension within a (generally wooden) rectangular frame (also called a sash or gate).

items.name: Sáb boga
items.text: Bow saw: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A bucksaw is a metal-framed crosscut saw in the shape of a bow with a coarse wide blade generally used with a sawbuck to cut logs or firewood to length (bucking).

items.name: Sáb dháu fhier
items.text: Two-man crosscut saw: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A crosscut saw (thwart saw) is any saw designed for cutting wood perpendicular to (across) the wood grain.

items.name: Sáb kuortaiti
items.text: Coping saw: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A coping saw is a type of bow saw used to cut intricate external shapes and interior cut-outs in woodworking or carpentry.

items.name: Sáb tienóin
items.text: Tenon saw: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A backsaw is any hand saw which has a stiffening rib on the edge opposite the cutting edge, enabling better control and more precise cutting than with other types of saws.

items.name: Heibil admaid
items.text: Wooden jack plane: earliest widespread use Roman (Rome). A hand plane is a tool for shaping wood using muscle power to force the cutting iron (blade) over the wood surface.

items.name: Spóksáb
items.text: Spokeshave: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A spokeshave is a hand tool used to shape and smooth woods in woodworking jobs such as making cart wheel spokes, chair legs, paddles, bows, and arrows.

items.name: Skian dháu láim
items.text: Drawknife: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A drawknife (drawing knife, draw shave, shaving knife) is a traditional woodworking hand tool used to shape wood by removing shavings.

items.name: Skoilteán
items.text: Froe: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A froe (or frow), shake axe or paling knife is a tool for splitting wood by cleaving it along the grain.

items.name: Droil bhoga
items.text: Bow drill: earliest widespread use c. 10000 BC (Worldwide). A bow drill is a simple hand-operated type of tool, consisting of a rod (the spindle or drill shaft) that is set in rapid rotary motion by means of a cord wrapped around it, kept taut by a bow which is pushed back and forth with one hand.

items.name: Biurán droileála
items.text: Brace and bit: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A brace is a hand tool used with a bit (drill bit or auger) to drill holes, usually in wood.

items.name: Taratán
items.text: Auger: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). An auger is a device to drill wood or other materials, consisting of a rotating metal shaft with a blade at the end that scrapes or cuts the wood.

items.name: Taratán bieg
items.text: Gimlet: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A gimlet is a hand tool for drilling small holes, mainly in wood, without splitting.

items.name: Droil láimi
items.text: Hand drill: earliest widespread use 1800s (Europe). A hand drill is the simplest primitive method to produce rapid rotary motion of a rod.

items.name: Ráspau
items.text: Rasp: earliest widespread use Medieval (Europe). A rasp is a coarse form of file used for shaping wood, metal, or other material.

items.name: Pouta glieú
items.text: Glue pot: earliest widespread use Ancient (Egypt). Animal glue is an adhesive that is created by prolonged boiling of animal connective tissue in a process called rendering.

items.name: Klampa
items.text: Clamp: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A clamp is a fastening device used to hold or secure objects tightly together to prevent movement or separation through the application of inward pressure.

items.name: Kapuld sábála
items.text: Sawhorse: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). In woodworking, a saw-horse or sawhorse (saw-buck, trestle, buck) is a trestle structure used to support a board or plank for sawing.

items.name: Binsi oibri
items.text: Workbench: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A workbench is a sturdy table at which manual work is done.

items.name: Meisín kasta admaid
items.text: Pole lathe: earliest widespread use c. 1300 BC (Egypt). A lathe () is a machine tool that rotates a workpiece about an axis of rotation to perform various operations such as cutting, sanding, knurling, drilling, deformation, facing, threading and turning, with tools that are applied to the workpiece to create an object with symmetry about that axis.

items.name: Skian chausta admaid
items.text: Wood turning gouge: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). Woodturning is the craft of using a wood lathe with hand-held tools to cut a shape that is symmetrical around the axis of rotation.

items.name: Tuo kóipéura
items.text: Cooper's adze: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A cooper is a craftsman who produces wooden casks, barrels, vats, buckets, tubs, troughs, and other similar containers from timber staves that were usually heated or steamed to make them pliable.

items.name: Tiumánaí fáindi bairildi
items.text: Barrel hoop driver: earliest widespread use Roman (Europe). A barrel or cask is a hollow cylindrical container with a bulging center, longer than it is wide.

items.name: Rod spókach
items.text: Spoked wheel: earliest widespread use c. 2000 BC (Eurasia). A wheel is a rotating component (typically circular in shape) intended to turn on an axle bearing.

items.name: Piend kleiti
items.text: Quill pen: earliest widespread use c. 600 (Europe). A quill is a writing tool made from a moulted flight feather of a large bird.

items.name: Piend giulkaí
items.text: Reed pen: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Egypt). A reed pen (Ancient Greek: κάλαμοι kalamoi; singular κάλαμος kalamos) or bamboo pen (traditional Chinese: 竹筆; simplified Chinese: 竹笔; pinyin: zhú bǐ) is a writing implement made by cutting and shaping a single reed straw or length of bamboo.

items.name: Stílies
items.text: Stylus: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Mesopotamia). A stylus is a writing implement or tool for scribing or marking into softer materials.

items.name: Táiebléad kéir
items.text: Wax tablet: earliest widespread use Ancient (Rome). A wax tablet is a tablet made of wood and covered with a layer of wax, often linked loosely to a cover tablet, as a "double-leaved"  diptych.

items.name: Skuob chailgrafachu
items.text: Calligraphy brush: earliest widespread use c. 300 BC (China). Chinese calligraphy is the writing of Chinese characters as an art form, combining visual art and interpretation of their literary meaning.

items.name: Dabach dúchu
items.text: Inkwell: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). An inkwell is a small jar or container, often made of glass, porcelain, silver, brass, or pewter, used for holding ink in a place convenient for the person who is writing.

items.name: Maidi dúchu
items.text: Ink stick: earliest widespread use c. 1000 BC (China). Inksticks (Chinese: 墨; pinyin: ) or ink cakes are a type of solid Chinese ink used traditionally in several Chinese, Japanese, and East Asian art forms such as calligraphy and brush painting.

items.name: Dúchlouch
items.text: Inkstone: earliest widespread use Han (China). An inkstone is a stone mortar for the grinding and containment of ink.

items.name: Piend kruoch
items.text: Steel nib pen: earliest widespread use 1822 (England). A dip pen is a writing instrument used to apply ink to paper by dipping into an inkwell.

items.name: Piend foinsi
items.text: Fountain pen: earliest widespread use 1827 (Romania). A fountain pen is a writing instrument that uses a metal nib to apply water-based ink to paper.

items.name: Piend luoidi
items.text: Pencil: earliest widespread use 1560s (Italy). A pencil ( ) is a writing or drawing implement with a solid pigment core in a protective casing that reduces the risk of core breakage and keeps it from marking the user's hand.

items.name: Staumpa séalaiti
items.text: Seal stamp: earliest widespread use Ancient (Worldwide). A seal is a device for making an impression in wax, clay, paper, or some other medium, including an embossment on paper, and is also the impression thus made.

items.name: Skrolda paupyrus
items.text: Papyrus scroll: earliest widespread use c. 3000 BC (Egypt). Papyrus ( pə-PY-rəs) is a substance used in ancient times as a writing surface.

items.name: Abakas
items.text: Abacus: earliest widespread use c. 2400 BC (Mesopotamia). An abacus (pl.

items.name: Pries priontálad
items.text: Printing press: earliest widespread use 1440 (Germany). A printing press is a machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto a surface made of paper, cloth, or a similar material.

items.name: Klóskríobán
items.text: Typewriter: earliest widespread use 1868 (USA). A typewriter is a mechanical or electromechanical machine for typing characters.
